title: ‘Everest: The Other Side’ — tragedy and triumph on the peaks of Nepal - Boston Herald
description: ‘Everest: The Other Side’ — tragedy and triumph on the peaks of Nepal  Boston Herald
publisher.title: Boston Herald
full_article:
Hike up and ski down was Jim Morrison’s relatively straightforward dream, albeit not on your typical ski hill.

Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson aspired to summit Mount Everest’s north side, something only five people had ever done. None had ever skied down it.

“Everest: The Other Side,” by “Free Solo” filmmakers Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, is the big-screen chronicle of Morrison and Nelson’s mission. Theirs is a quixotic aspiration: climb the world’s highest peak and then coast down.

But “Everest: The Other Side” is as much a document of tragedy and grief as it is one of extreme sport. On a similar expedition in 2022 while biding their time for Everest, Morrison and Nelson — partners in love and adventure — reached the top of a Nepalese mountain. But after just a few turns on her skis, a sheet of snow dislodged underneath Nelson. She died in the avalanche.

Nelson’s death reverberated through the mountaineering world and it reshaped the film Vasarhelyi and Chin were making. In “Free Solo,” which documents Alex Honnold ascending El Capitan in Yosemite without ropes or a harness, the filmmakers had to contemplate the possibility that Honnold might fall to his death.

In “Everest,” that awful possibility comes to pass. Nelson’s fatal fall, as well as Morrison’s recovery of her body two days later, is captured with agonizing IMAX clarity.

“This movie, the worst happened,” Vasarhelyi says in a brief moment on screen.

Risk tolerance is a common topic for Vasarhelyi and Chin, filmmakers who have intrepidly fused nature documentaries with adventure drama. Chin is himself a decorated climber; he summited and skied down the south face of Everest in 2006.

But in “Everest,” questioning whether it’s worth it is front and center. The movie lingers on the moments when Morrison and his team leave their homes, parting with children for two-month stints during which they’ll risk their lives on desolate peaks on the other side of the world. When Nelson dies, she leaves behind two boys. As the years tick on in the documentary, we watch them grow up without their mother.

Yet within months of her death, Morrison, from his lakeside Tahoe home, resolves to push ahead with the Everest climb. Tragedy isn’t new to him. Years earlier, he lost his wife, Katie, and two children, Wyatt and Hannah, in a plane crash. After first finding a walk down the driveway an insurmountable hike, Morrison resolves to live for them.

So his aim to reach the top of Everest and ski down may be a daredevil feat, but it’s also a grieving, heavy-hearted quest. He describes his yearning to ride down “the raddest ski line in the world.” But what’s compelling him is also something that can’t be easily articulated.

Deciding to continue with the project is its own debate for Chin and Vasarhelyi. They have two children of their own. Their proximity to extreme expeditions has already brought tragedy close to home. “How many people who have eaten at our dinner table have died?” Vasarhelyi asks him. The couple divorced in 2025, though their separation goes unmentioned in the film.

While these debates are often present in the documentary, “Everest: The Other Side” grows increasingly shy of them. The higher Morrison climbs, the less inquisitive the movie gets. On the first attempted ascent, some of the Sherpas grow wary of the risks involved. Their sensible hesitations don’t put Morrison, handsomely outfitted by his North Face sponsor, in the best light.

By the time Morrison realizes his dream, it feels as though many have, off camera, moved on with their lives. The families back home fall out of the movie. “Everest: The Other Side” becomes a mournful and increasingly solitary march.

Maybe that’s appropriate. Morrison’s extreme compulsion inevitably pulls him away from us, leaving behind a more disquieting film. Even he can’t help but notice while hiking up that the snow conditions he’ll be skiing down are rock hard and terrible. The descent, lasting four hours, is a feat of skill, perseverance and bravery. Even on a bad day, he’d have to grant, the skiing would have been better back home.

(“Everest: The Other Side” contains thematic material and brief strong language)

title: Explained: The leaked WhatsApp chats that have shaken Nepal’s judiciary - The Kathmandu Post
description: Explained: The leaked WhatsApp chats that have shaken Nepal’s judiciary  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
On Thursday, the Naya Patrika daily published a bombshell report detailing a WhatsApp exchange between Supreme Court Justice Hari Prasad Phuyal and Inam Sapkota, a man accused of using connections with powerful figures to influence state institutions.

The revelation has brought Nepal’s judiciary under renewed scrutiny, raising questions about possible attempts to influence court proceedings, Phuyal’s own conduct and the deeper institutional fault lines within Nepal’s highest court.

Here’s what you need to know about the unfolding controversy, explained in five points.

1. What do the leaked WhatsApp exchanges reveal?

The messages show Sapkota sending Phuyal a screenshot of businessman Rohit Gupta’s habeas corpus petition, followed by a request to dismiss it, invoking Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s interest in the matter.

“Please stop this, sir,” Sapkota reportedly wrote. “The prime minister is also interested in this matter. Please dismiss it.”

Hours later, Phuyal replied that there were grounds to release Gupta and that the court had ordered him to post Rs20 million in bail. He also shared a link to the court order and proposed meeting Sapkota at Hotel Himalaya the following evening. The exchange has raised questions about why a sitting justice was communicating with an alleged fixer about a pending case.

2. Who is Inam Sapkota, and why is he under investigation?

Sapkota, 30, came under police scrutiny after investigators examining the phone of former chief justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana found repeated calls between the two. Police detained Sapkota at Tribhuvan International Airport on September 27, as he was preparing to travel to India.

Further examination of his electronic devices reportedly revealed communications with serving and former judges, senior police officials, politicians, lawmakers and lawyers. Investigators suspect he acted as an intermediary for officials seeking promotions and for people seeking favourable outcomes in court cases.

His reported connections with former chief justice Rana, businessman Deepak Bhatta and other influential figures have widened the investigation. Police are also examining possible money-laundering links.

3. What has Phuyal said about his dealings with Sapkota?

Phuyal has acknowledged exchanging messages and meeting Sapkota at Hotel Himalaya, a five-star facility about two kilometres from the Supreme Court. He says Sapkota initially approached him claiming to represent the prime minister and offering reassurance amid rumours that some justices could face impeachment following Manoj Kumar Sharma’s appointment as chief justice.

According to Phuyal, Sapkota subsequently began to bring up pending cases, including the Nepali Congress leadership dispute and cases involving businessman Bhatta. Phuyal says he and several other justices eventually grew suspicious, discussed Sapkota’s conduct among themselves and reported their concerns to the prime minister’s secretariat, the police chief and the army chief.

Phuyal maintains that he did not act on Sapkota’s request in Gupta’s case and that the decision to release Gupta on bail was based on the merits of the case. He denies financial dealings or any improper arrangement. But he has not explained why he felt obliged to justify a decision his bench took to an individual with an interest in the case.

His statement leaves other important questions unanswered: Why did he rely on someone whose claim to represent the prime minister had not been verified? Why was a hotel meeting considered appropriate? What exactly was discussed, and when did he first suspect Sapkota's intentions?

The questions have acquired added significance because Phuyal later sat on a bench that dismissed a habeas corpus petition filed by Sapkota’s wife challenging his detention. The bench, which included Justice Sunil Pokharel, rejected the petition on October 9.

4. Why has Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma also come under scrutiny?

The controversy extends beyond Phuyal. Separate documents reportedly recovered from Sapkota’s phone and circulated publicly refer to deposits into bank accounts associated with Chief Justice Sharma, Rastriya Swatantra Party lawmaker Bishwaraj Pokharel and senior police officer Banshiraj Dahal. The records mention deposits totalling 198,333 in unspecified currency over three months and a request for a further $7,500, with payments directed to accounts held by Sapkota’s relatives.

Sharma has denied knowing Sapkota or having any direct or indirect contact with him. Dahal was dismissed following an investigation into his communications with Sapkota and a late-night visit to former chief justice Cholendra Shumsher Rana after the latter was taken into police custody.

The alleged transactions have not been independently established as bribes or conclusively linked to the individuals named. The Nepal Bar Association has called for an impartial, evidence-based investigation into the revelations.

5. How does this controversy fit into the Supreme Court’s wider crisis?

The latest revelations come amid months of tension within the judiciary. In September, police took former chief justice Rana from his home , initially describing the action as an arrest before saying he had been moved to a secure location because of a security threat. The Supreme Court’s subsequent full-court statement condemned arbitrary executive action but also pledged to prevent both external and internal influence in judicial proceedings. The reference to internal influence exposed concerns about the role of former office-holders and divisions within the court.

The tensions also stem from Sharma’s appointment as chief justice in May, when the Constitutional Council bypassed three more senior justices, including Phuyal, without setting out clear criteria. Disagreements over judicial appointments, the formation of the Constitutional Bench, transfers and promotions have further strained relations.

The Sapkota revelations have brought these institutional fault lines into the fore. The challenge now is not simply to determine whether individual judges or officials engaged in wrongdoing, but also to establish credible safeguards against intermediaries seeking to influence judicial decisions. The credibility of the Supreme Court will depend on whether it can address both questions through a transparent and impartial process.

title: UN extends LDC graduation timeframe for Nepal and Bangladesh - The Rising Nepal
description: UN extends LDC graduation timeframe for Nepal and Bangladesh  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 30: The United Nations General Assembly has unanimously passed a proposal to extend the preparation period necessary for Nepal and Bangladesh to graduate from the least developed country (LDCs) status until November 24, 2029.

The UN's 81st General Assembly meeting on Thursday made this decision, according to the Permanent Mission of Nepal to the United Nations, New York.

With this, Nepal now has extra time to carry out necessary structural and institutional reforms more effectively before being upgraded from the list of least developed countries.

Nepal has expressed its commitment to use this period for increasing production capacity, strengthening institutions, and pursuing economic and social transformation.

It is believed that the additional time received from the UN General Assembly will help Nepal easily, sustainably, and irreversibly achieve the goal of graduating from the LDC status.(RSS)

title: Festivities far from families - Nepali Times
description: Festivities far from families  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Tika Day last week was not the best day for most Nepalis working in Doha, especially those who had to work long shifts at a time when most at home would be celebrating Dasain with much fanfare.

But away from loved ones, they still found some time last week, either in their quarters, work, or Nepali restaurants to celebrate the festival season.

A Nepal restaurant operator making selroti during Dasain last week. She had sold around 300 selroti by 4PM.

Qatar is home to an estimated 400,000 Nepalis, making it the second largest population non-nationals in the country after India. For the majority, going back home in Dasain is a privilege, or is not affordable. Many who left Nepal to work here have not been able to celebrate the three festivals for years.

In Nepali neighbourhoods across Doha, the longing for home during the holiday season was tempered somewhat by the aroma of familiar food at Nepali restaurants.

Elsewhere in the city, a delivery driver parked his bike while waiting on orders to give a quick call to family back home on Tika day. They miss him. He misses them.

A virtual tika ceremony was held over videocall on Messenger. Blessings were transmuted from thousands of kilometers away, but the busy street was not the place to conduct the ceremony. After a brief chitchat, both sides hung up.

The driver put his phone away, then got back to business. There was stuff to deliver, and money to be made.

A restaurant operator wraps selroti as a food delivery rider reaches the restaurant to pick up the order. The stream of orders kept coming throughout the night.

The riyal the primary reason many here left our homes, and with it, our sense of belonging. Last week, the Dasain dakshina here was given in riyals. Seeing a tika mark on a one riyal note made many homesick, and soon it will be Tihar when they will miss their sisters and brothers back home.

Guests visited Nepali restaurants before and after their shifts to briefly celebrate Dasain.

title: Nepal comes up with four proposals for dealing with mountain crises, 53 nations back them - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal comes up with four proposals for dealing with mountain crises, 53 nations back them  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 30: Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, has said that the crises caused by climate change in the Himalayan region are not confined within the geographical boundaries of just one country.

At a high-level regional dialogue organized on Thursday in Bangkok by the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP) and the Government of Nepal under the title 'From Everest to the Sea,' he said that global cooperation is necessary for mountain conservation.

Minister Shrestha's secretariat has stated that representatives from 53 countries have supported the four proposals that Nepal presented to the international community to reduce the impacts of climate change and manage cross-border disaster risks.

Nepal has emphasized the need to develop a multi-hazard early warning system based on satellites, artificial intelligence (AI), and modern technology, through collaboration between international space agencies, scientific institutions, and the government, to monitor risky mountain slopes and glaciers.

Minister Shrestha also mentioned that Prime Minister Balendra Shah proposed the 'Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism' for coordinating information exchange, glacier monitoring, and early warning systems in the Himalayan region.

Minister Shrestha emphasized that immediate financial assistance should be made available for disaster risk reduction, preparedness, and recovery, and that it should be accessible and grant-based.

He said that in high Himalayan areas, monitoring and early warning should be supported through grants, not loans, and investments in riverside hydropower projects to border towns should be managed by considering the risks from the source to the sea.((RSS)

title: TikTok removes more than 2 million videos from Nepal in three months - OnlineKhabar English News
description: TikTok removes more than 2 million videos from Nepal in three months  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Photo by Solen Feyissa on Unsplash

Kathmandu, October 30

TikTok has released its Community Guidelines Enforcement Report for the second quarter of 2026 (April to June), showing that it removed 2,036,191 videos from Nepal for violating its Community Guidelines during the three months.

According to the report, the removed videos accounted for 0.4 per cent of all videos published in Nepal. The platform identified and removed 99.5 per cent of the videos before users reported them.

A total of 92.3 per cent of the videos that violated the guidelines were removed within 24 hours. Following further review, 33,503 videos were restored.

Globally, TikTok removed 188,298,141 videos during the period, accounting for approximately 0.5 per cent of all content uploaded to the platform.

Of these, 183,344,707 videos were removed using automated detection technology, according to TikTok.

During the same period, TikTok removed 146,807,400 fake accounts. It also removed 26,840,767 accounts suspected of belonging to users under the age of 13. In addition, 278,384,463 comments were removed for violating the Community Guidelines.

Of the content published during the period, 2.4 per cent of live content was placed under review. As an enforcement measure, TikTok issued warnings to or removed monetisation privileges from 767,201,093 live sessions and 267,801,135 live creators.

title: Balen-led govt scores diplomatic success as UN grants Nepal three more years for LDC graduation - Khabarhub
description: Balen-led govt scores diplomatic success as UN grants Nepal three more years for LDC graduation  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Balendra Shah-led government has achieved a significant diplomatic success by securing an additional three years for Nepal to prepare for graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category, following unanimous approval by the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).

Under Resolution 81/L.8, adopted during the Assembly’s 81st session in New York, Nepal and Bangladesh have been granted an extended preparatory period until November 24, 2029, postponing their previously scheduled graduation date of November 24, 2026.

The decision marks an important achievement for the Shah government, which formally approached the United Nations in May 2026, seeking additional time to address the country’s economic vulnerabilities, strengthen productive capacity and prepare institutions for the challenges associated with graduation.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal conveyed Nepal’s request through a letter dated May 13 to the chairperson of the UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP), seeking a three-year postponement.

The government argued that graduating under the prevailing economic circumstances could expose Nepal to considerable risks, particularly the possible withdrawal of international trade preferences and other support measures available to LDCs.

Foreign Ministry has earlier said the request was based on several economic and geopolitical concerns, including the effects of conflicts in West Asia, disruptions to international supply chains, declining growth prospects and vulnerabilities in remittance-dependent sectors.

The government also cited a World Bank projection that placed Nepal’s economic growth at 2.3 percent for the current fiscal year. Officials warned that the withdrawal of duty-free and quota-free market access following graduation could put employment in productive sectors at risk, with potential losses estimated at up to 35 percent.

The CDP subsequently conducted a crisis assessment under its enhanced monitoring mechanism and concluded that extending Nepal’s preparatory period would be appropriate, provided the government developed and implemented a clear, time-bound plan to revise and reprioritise its Smooth Transition Strategy.

The UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), in a decision adopted on July 21, took note of the committee’s conclusions and recommended that the General Assembly take a decision before Nepal’s original graduation deadline.

The General Assembly’s unanimous endorsement of the extension represents an important outcome of Nepal’s diplomatic engagement and efforts to secure international recognition of its economic challenges.

Nepal had originally been scheduled to graduate in November 2026 following a General Assembly decision in 2021. At that time, the country received an exceptional five-year preparatory period instead of the standard three years because of the socioeconomic disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

The latest extension provides the government with additional time to strengthen economic resilience, improve competitiveness, expand productive capacity and prepare for the eventual withdrawal of LDC-specific international support measures.

The decision is particularly significant given the country’s fragile post-pandemic recovery, exposure to climate-related risks, dependence on remittances and vulnerability to external economic shocks.

However, the additional time also brings greater responsibility. The government will need to accelerate implementation of Nepal’s Smooth Transition Strategy, strengthen institutional capacity, diversify exports, improve industrial productivity and reduce structural economic vulnerabilities.

The extension should therefore be viewed not simply as a postponement of graduation but as an opportunity for the Balen Shah government to build stronger economic foundations and ensure that Nepal’s eventual transition from LDC status is sustainable and beneficial.

An Opportunity to Attract Investment and Strengthen Competitiveness

The extended preparatory period also offers Nepal an opportunity to transform potential graduation-related challenges into economic opportunities.

One important priority will be improving the country’s investment climate and attracting greater foreign direct investment (FDI). Graduation from the LDC category can strengthen Nepal’s international economic standing, provided it is accompanied by improvements in governance, policy predictability, financial transparency and institutional performance.

The government can use the additional time to strengthen intellectual property protection, improve the business environment, explore sovereign credit-rating opportunities and develop financial instruments that help manage foreign exchange risks.

Another priority is strengthening domestic industries and export competitiveness. Nepal will need to reduce its reliance on preferential trade arrangements by improving productivity, adopting modern technologies, upgrading logistics and increasing value addition.

Sectors such as hydropower, tourism, digital services and high-value agriculture offer opportunities to expand exports, generate employment and diversify the economy.

The eventual reduction of preferential trade access also makes proactive bilateral and regional trade diplomacy increasingly important. Nepal will need to explore preferential and free trade arrangements with major trading partners to maintain the competitiveness of its exports.

Moving Towards Sustainable and Investment-Led Development

Graduation may also gradually change the nature of international development financing available to Nepal. As traditional concessional assistance becomes less accessible, the country will need to strengthen its capacity to mobilise alternative sources of development finance.

The extended period could help Nepal develop the institutional and technical capacity to access climate finance, blended financing, adaptation funds and sovereign green bonds.

This would be particularly important for financing climate-resilient infrastructure, renewable energy, disaster preparedness and sustainable development projects.

At the same time, Nepal needs to shift its economic growth model from one heavily driven by consumption and remittance inflows towards domestic production, industrial development, investment and employment generation.

Strengthening fiscal transparency, maintaining macroeconomic stability, improving the ease of doing business and accelerating institutional reforms will be essential to achieving this transition.

Implementation Will Determine Success

Nepal’s Smooth Transition Strategy, which outlines the country’s preparations for graduation, must now become the central framework for utilising the extended period.

The government will need to accelerate reforms, strengthen productive and institutional capacity, diversify exports, improve industrial competitiveness and develop alternative sources of financing.

Continued engagement with multilateral institutions and major trading partners will also be necessary to secure favourable trade arrangements and minimise disruptions when LDC-specific benefits are eventually phased out.

The extension should therefore be viewed not simply as a postponement of graduation but as a strategic opportunity for Nepal to strengthen its economic foundations.

For the Balen Shah government, securing the additional three years represents an important diplomatic achievement. Its longer-term success, however, will depend on how effectively the government uses this opportunity to build a resilient, competitive and self-sustaining economy.

Ultimately, Nepal’s graduation from the LDC category should mark not merely the end of preferential international support, but the beginning of a more productive, investment-driven and economically resilient development pathway.

title: Nepal seeks recognition for six more 8,000-metre peaks - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal seeks recognition for six more 8,000-metre peaks  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal is seeking international recognition for six additional Himalayan peaks above 8,000 metres, a move that would increase the country’s internationally recognised eight-thousanders from eight to 14.

Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel and Nepal Mountaineering Association (NMA) President Fur Gelje Sherpa presented the proposal at the 2026 general assembly of the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), held in Kathmandu.

Speaking at the assembly on Thursday evening, Paudel said Nepal was pursuing international recognition for the six peaks as independent mountains above 8,000 metres. Sherpa also addressed the UIAA executive board, urging it to formally assess the proposed peaks and grant them separate international recognition.

Nepal already lists 14 mountains above 8,000 metres in its national records, following a revision by the Department of Tourism in 2025. However, the international mountaineering community currently recognises only eight in Nepal. The NMA is seeking to have the remaining six added to the internationally recognised list.

If the proposal is accepted, Nepal would account for 14 of the world's 20 internationally recognised mountains above 8,000 metres, up from its current share of eight among the global total of 14.

Four of the proposed peaks are in the Kanchenjunga massif and two in the Everest-Lhotse region.

The four in the Kanchenjunga region are Kanchenjunga South (8,476 metres), Kanchenjunga Central (8,473 metres), Yalung Khang (8,505 metres) and Yalung Khang West (8,077 metres). The other two are Lhotse Middle (8,410 metres) and Lhotse Shar (8,400 metres).

Sherpa said each peak had its own name, geographical identity and distinct route to the summit. Reaching one summit did not mean climbing another, he argued, and each should therefore be assessed as an independent mountaineering destination.

“The aim of seeking separate recognition for these peaks is not simply to increase the number of mountains on the international list,” he said at the assembly. “Their distinct identities, local names, geographical features and separate routes to their summits deserve fair and professional assessment.”

He said climbing above 8,000 metres involved exceptional challenges and that reaching each distinct summit should count as an independent mountaineering achievement. Such climbs require extraordinary physical endurance, technical skills, experience and meticulous preparation, he said.

Sherpa said former NMA presidents and executive committee members had been raising the issue for years, but their efforts had yet to secure the expected international recognition or response.

This time, the association has formed a team of experts to advance the proposal. A five-member team led by Madhusudan Adhikari made a detailed presentation outlining the grounds and justification for recognising the six peaks separately.

Paudel said international recognition would strengthen Nepal’s identity as a country of high mountains and open up further opportunities in mountaineering, adventure tourism, Himalayan research and tourism promotion.

“We believe this will also help establish Nepal as a leading destination for the world's highest mountains,” he said.

He said international discussions on mountain recognition and classification should also address climate-related threats to the Himalayas, the conservation of their natural resources and the livelihoods of mountain communities.

Around 60 representatives of mountaineering federations, experts and other stakeholders from countries including Canada, India, Malta, Argentina, the Netherlands, South Africa, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Belgium, the United States, France, Germany, Japan and Italy are attending the UIAA's 2026 general assembly in Kathmandu.

KATHMANDU: US Chargé d’Affaires Megan Bouldin met Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel on Friday to discuss strengthening bilateral cooperation in education and sports, with a particular focus on expanding US exchange programmes and advancing sports diplomacy.

During the meeting, Bouldin highlighted the valuable contributions of Nepali participants in US exchange programmes, including the Fulbright Programme, who returned home and applied their knowledge and experience to Nepal’s education sector.

title: Nepal, India agree to tighten border checks, expand surveillance - WION
description: Nepal, India agree to tighten border checks, expand surveillance  WION
publisher.title: WION
full_article:
Nepal and India have agreed to tighten security checks, increase coordinated border patrols and strengthen information sharing to prevent cross-border crimes along their shared border. The agreement was reached at the three-day 10th Nepal-India Coordination Meeting between the Armed Police Force (APF) Nepal and India's Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), which concluded in Kathmandu.

According to a statement issued by the APF, both sides agreed to strengthen cooperation at the strategic, operational and field levels to control illegal activities including the unauthorised movement of third-country nationals through the open border.

The two security agencies agreed to tighten document verification and security checks at border checkpoints, conduct coordinated patrols in the No-Man's Land and promptly exchange information about suspicious individuals. They also agreed to continue joint efforts to remove unauthorised farming, encroachments and illegal structures from the border strip. Both sides will strengthen field-level coordination for the maintenance, repair and reconstruction of boundary pillars in line with decisions of the Boundary Working Group (BWG) and the Survey Officials Committee (SOC).

The meeting also discussed introducing modern technology to improve border surveillance, including CCTV cameras to monitor the No-Man's Land, luggage scanners and walk-through metal detectors at major checkpoints and greater use of drones in their respective territories.

Cyclone Arnab-induced weather pattern brings snowfall and rain in Nepal

First Published: 30th October, 2026 16:18 IST

Many have taken shelter in hotels and settlements along the trekking routes, with accommodation facilities reportedly filled.

Written By Northeast Live Digital Desk SHARE IT NOW







The weather pattern induced by Cyclone Arnab has brought snowfall and rain in various parts of Nepal. The heavy snowfall in the high-lying areas has left hundreds of trekkers and tourists stranded, forcing them to take shelter in hotels and lodges at high altitudes.

Tourism officials confirmed that heavy snowfall in higher elevations and freezing temperatures in lower areas have disrupted trekking activities, leaving tourists travelling to and returning from the base camps unable to continue their journeys. Many have taken shelter in hotels and settlements along the trekking routes, with accommodation facilities reportedly filled.

Hundreds of domestic and foreign trekkers have been left stranded along the Kanchenjunga trail, forcing them to take shelter in hotels, averting their movement. The area has experienced light rainfall, rising temperatures and snowfall in higher mountain areas.

Tourist numbers have increased in settlements along both the northern and southern Kanchenjunga base camp routes. These include Italitar, Lamatar, Amjilesa, Thangim, Gyabla, Phale, Ghunsa, Khambachen and Lonak in the north, and Yamphudin, Naya Jhoreni, Torongden, Seram and Ramje in the south.

Meanwhile, a group of foreign tourists heading towards Makalu base camp via the Lumbasumba Pass has been held up in Olangchungola, as per the officials. About half of the tourists in Olangchungola are heading towards Makalu base camp via the Lumbasumba route. Domestic tourists travelling to Singje through Olangchungola have also been unable to proceed because of the adverse weather.

The Armed Police Force personnel deployed for border security and the local ward office have issued notices advising people to remain in safe locations until weather conditions improve.

Chief District Officer Umesh Kumar Dahal said no disaster-related incidents had been reported in the district so far. He confirmed that approximately 250 domestic and foreign tourists were staying in settlements and hotels across the Kanchenjunga region, particularly in Olangchungola, Ghunsa and Yamphudin.

Authorities have advised tourists to prioritise safety and resume trekking only after carefully assessing weather conditions. Necessary precautions have been taken in coordination with security agencies and local governments. Residents have also been alerted, Dahal said.

The capital, Kathmandu, also received rainfall overnight, clearing the skyline of the valley that is surrounded by hills and mountains. Though the skyline is cleared of dust and pollution, the capital is still shrouded by rain-induced clouds. (ANI)

Cyclone Arnab continues to affect Nepal, with rainfall reported in several parts of the country, including Kathmandu and other areas of Bagmati Province. Snowfall is also forecast in high-altitude regions.

According to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, moderate rain and snowfall, accompanied by thunderstorms, are expected in several parts of the country today and tomorrow. Heavy to very heavy precipitation is possible at some locations in Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces.

The Roshi weather station in Kavrepalanchok recorded 50.2 millimetres of rainfall in the 24 hours up to Friday morning.

The department has warned of heavy snowfall and snowstorms in high Himalayan areas. Tourists and trekkers have been advised to avoid high-altitude journeys and remain in safe locations until conditions improve.

The adverse conditions may disrupt road and air transport, agriculture and daily life.

The effects of Cyclone Arnab and associated rainfall are expected to ease from Saturday afternoon, the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology said.

The India Meteorological Department reported that Cyclone Arnab weakened into a well-marked low-pressure area over central Chhattisgarh and adjoining Odisha on October 29, and is expected to weaken further.

Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka brought their tourism offerings to Brussels on 29 October 2026, presenting journeys ranging from Himalayan trekking and spiritual retreats to island discoveries and coastal escapes. Jointly organised by the four countries’ embassies at De Warande, “From Mountain Peaks to Coastal Shores” placed hospitality, cultural heritage and responsible tourism at the centre of its second edition.

The gathering built on the inaugural event, held at the same venue in July 2025 under the title “The Enchanting Trio”. With Nepal joining Bhutan, the Maldives and Sri Lanka, this year’s edition broadened the geographical scope while maintaining a shared focus on tourism that supports communities and protects the places travellers come to experience.

EU highlights tourism’s role in sustainable development

Guest of honour Dominic Porter, Deputy Managing Director for Asia and the Pacific at the European External Action Service, connected the destinations’ presentations with the European Union’s work on sustainable development. He described tourism as a source of employment, cultural exchange and conservation, while outlining EU support for businesses, heritage protection and greener tourism practices across the region.

“Tourism still holds much untapped potential to promote connections between people,” Porter said. He highlighted assistance for local guesthouses and safari vessels in the Maldives, cultural heritage and sustainable tourism projects in Nepal, and support for Sri Lankan tourism businesses recovering from economic crises.

© Gerard Huiting

Bhutan: kindness, mindfulness and a lighter footprint

For Bhutan’s Ambassador Tshoki Choden, the visitor experience begins with something less tangible than scenery: the freedom to feel welcome and at ease. “One of the greatest luxuries of travel is being able to let your guard down,” she said, presenting kindness and hospitality as defining features of a journey through the Himalayan kingdom.

Choden linked that welcome to Bhutan’s approach to development, describing mindfulness as a principle that shapes both everyday life and tourism policy. She highlighted the country’s constitutional commitment to maintaining at least 60% forest cover and its high-value, low-impact tourism model, which seeks to protect cultural heritage and the environment while benefiting local communities.

“We believe that not everything has to be conquered to prosper,” she said, referring to Bhutan’s unconquered mountains. Her invitation also extended to the country’s food, including its famously fiery combination of chillies and cheese, and to a broader exploration of what happiness means beyond material possessions.

© Embassy of Bhutan to the Kingdom of Belgium

Nepal: adventure and spiritual discovery

Nepal’s Ambassador Sewa Lamsal presented a destination where adventure, cultural diversity and spiritual heritage sit alongside one another. Moving from the Himalayas to the country’s southern plains, she described opportunities for trekking, rafting, paragliding and mountain biking, as well as quieter experiences centred on meditation and reflection.

“Welcoming visitors with respect and generosity is perhaps the greatest gift people carry home,” Lamsal said. She highlighted Lumbini, the birthplace of the Buddha, alongside Nepal’s temples, monasteries and pilgrimage traditions, inviting travellers to explore a country whose appeal extends well beyond its best-known mountain routes.

Well-being was another theme of her address, with Lamsal encouraging visitors to discover Nepal through cultural immersion, mindfulness and time in nature. She also invited investors and business leaders to explore opportunities in the tourism sector, placing local hospitality at the heart of its future development.

© Embassy of Nepal to the Kingdom of Belgium

Sri Lanka: an island of discovery and serendipity

Sri Lanka’s Ambassador Chandana Weerasena drew on his country’s long history of welcoming travellers, describing an island shaped by maritime connections and encounters between cultures. “We continue building bridges and sharing the very best of what our countries have to offer,” he said, introducing a destination he associated with discovery and serendipity.

His presentation reflected the breadth of Sri Lanka’s appeal, from its Indian Ocean setting to its cultural heritage. Travel Tomorrow’s reporting has explored that variety through experiences such as Isiwara Ayurvedic Village in Matale, where spice gardens, cooking and traditional practices offer visitors an introduction to local knowledge and daily life.

The country has also taken steps to encourage international arrivals. As Travel Tomorrow reported in May, Sri Lanka introduced a free Electronic Travel Authorization scheme for tourists from 40 countries, including Belgium, while retaining the requirement to obtain authorisation before travelling.

Sri Lanka introduces free ETA scheme for tourists from 40 countries

Maldives prepares for ITB Berlin 2027 spotlight

Represented by Ambassador Fathimath Dhiyana Saeed, the Maldives participated as it prepares for a prominent place on the international tourism calendar. The island nation will be the Official Host Country of ITB Berlin 2027, taking place from 16 to 18 March, providing a platform to showcase its hospitality, cultural diversity and tourism experiences to the global travel industry.

The preparations form part of a wider promotional push that includes Visit Maldives Year 2027. Alongside its established luxury offering, developments such as a proposed electric hydrofoil boat network illustrate efforts to improve connections between islands while reducing the environmental impact of transport.

A shared commitment to responsible travel

Across the four presentations, hospitality emerged as the common thread linking very different landscapes and travel experiences. Porter’s closing message returned to the importance of ensuring that tourism benefits the people and ecosystems on which it depends: “You can count on us to accompany you on this journey every step of the way.”
